# Volume 3 — Chapter I The Shadow of Change

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“Harvest is ended and summer is gone,” quoted Nell Harcourt, looking out over the harvested fields in a dreamlike way. Isolde Pembroke and she had been gathering apples in the orchard at Grey Shutters, but they were currently taking a break from their work in a sunlit nook, where light swarms of thistledown floated past carried by a breeze that remained summer-sweet with the fragrance of ferns from the Whispering Wood.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0000 }

Yet all details of the surrounding countryside proclaimed that it was autumn. Deeply and hollowly, the ocean resounded far off, while the empty, withered fields were draped in golden rod, purple asters of an otherworldly shade spilled through the brook valley beneath Grey Shutters, and the Lake of Glassy Waters possessed a blue—blue—blue hue; this was not spring's shifting shade of blue, nor summer's light azure, but a distinct, unchanging, peaceful blue, appearing as though the water had outlived every emotional shift and phase to rest in a calmness undisturbed by fleeting dreams.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0001 }

“It’s been a pleasant summer,” Isolde stated, a smile on her face as she turned the newly acquired ring on her left hand. “And the crowning moment of it all appeared to be Miss Rosalind’s wedding. I imagine that Mr. and Mrs. Stanhope have reached the Pacific coast by this time.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0002 }

“It appears to me that their absence has lasted long enough for a journey around the globe,” Nell sighed.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0003 }

“It seems impossible that a mere week has passed since their wedding. Everything is different now. With Miss Rosalind along with Mr. and Mrs. Wace departed, the manse appears so desolate with all its shutters drawn! Passing by it yesterday evening, I felt as though every single occupant within had perished.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0004 }

“We will not ever obtain a different minister who is as pleasant as Mr. Wace,” Isolde stated, possessing a dismal certainty. “I imagine that various supplies will be provided to us during this winter, while preaching will be entirely absent for half of the Sundays. Furthermore, with both you and Hugh having departed—the time is going to be dreadfully boring.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0005 }

“Gideon will be present,” suggested Nell in a cunning manner.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0006 }

“When is Mrs. Sowerby going to move up?” asked Isolde, acting as though she had failed to hear what Nell said.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0007 }

“Tomorrow. I am pleased that she is arriving—though it signifies yet another shift. Thirza and I removed all the contents from the spare room yesterday. Would you believe that I disliked doing so? Naturally, it was foolish—yet it felt almost as though we were perpetrating sacrilege. To me, that ancient spare room has perpetually felt like a sacred space. As a youngster, I regarded it as the most marvelous chamber on earth. You recall my overwhelming longing to spend a night in a spare room bed—yet certainly not the one at Grey Shutters. Oh, absolutely not there! It would have been far too terrifying—awe would have kept me awake the entire night. Whenever Thirza dispatched me there on a task, I never simply walked across that space—indeed, I crept on tiptoe and suspended my breathing, just as if I were inside a church, feeling a sense of ease only upon leaving it. Hanging there, positioned on either side of the looking glass, were the portraits of Laurence Whitefield and the Duke of Wellington, who glowered at me with great severity the whole time I remained inside, particularly if I took the risk of glancing into the glass, which happened to be the sole mirror in the dwelling that failed to distort my features slightly. It was a constant mystery to me how Thirza possessed the audacity to clean that space. Yet at present, it has not merely been tidied, but emptied completely. Laurence Whitefield and the Duke have been banished to the hallway on the upper floor. ‘So passes the glory of this world,’” Nell finished, offering a chuckle that carried a subtle tone of sorrow. Having our former sanctuaries defiled is never an agreeable experience, even after we have advanced beyond them.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0008 }

“When you depart, I will feel terribly lonely,” Isolde lamented as she had done a hundred times before. “And it’s unbearable that your departure is next week!”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0009 }

“However, we remain united even now,” Nell remarked brightly. “We cannot permit the coming week to take away the happiness of the present one. Despising the prospect of departing is something I feel personally—my home and I share such a strong bond. Speaking about feeling isolated! I am the one who ought to lament. You will remain in this place surrounded by a multitude of your former companions—and Gideon! Whereas I will find myself solitary in the midst of unfamiliar people, without a single acquaintance!”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0010 }

“With the exception of Hugh—and Wilfred Mott,” Isolde remarked, copying the italics and stealthiness of Nell.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0011 }

“Wilfred Mott will be a great comfort, of course,” Nell concurred with sarcasm; at which point the two frivolous young women broke into laughter. Isolde was fully aware of Nell’s opinion regarding Wilfred Mott; nevertheless, even after several private conversations, she was uncertain of Nell’s true feelings about Hugh Carrow. Naturally, Nell was equally unaware of them herself.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0012 }

“The boys might be getting on the ship at the far end of Portmaris, for all that I am aware,” Nell continued. “I feel happy that I am traveling to Wexcombe, and I am certain that I will enjoy it given some time. However, for the initial few weeks I am positive I will not. I will not even possess the consolation of anticipating the weekend trip home, as was the case when I attended Regent’s. Christmas will appear to be a thousand years in the future.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0013 }

“All is altering—or about to alter,” Isolde stated mournfully. “Nell, I possess a sense that conditions are not ever going to be what they were,”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0014 }

“It seems we have reached a point where our paths separate,” Nell observed meditatively. “It was inevitable that we would reach this stage. Isolde, do you believe that adulthood is actually as pleasant as we assumed it was going to be during our childhood?”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0015 }

“I don’t know—there are some nice things about it,” Isolde replied, touching her ring once more with that faint smile that invariably caused Nell to feel abruptly excluded and lacking in experience. “But there are so many puzzling things, too. At times I feel as though becoming an adult simply scares me—and during those moments I would do whatever it takes to be a young girl once more.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0016 }

“Eventually, I expect we will become accustomed to adulthood,” Nell remarked in a cheerful manner. “As time goes on, it won’t hold quite as many surprises—even if, when all is said and done, I suspect those very surprises are what make life interesting. Isolde, we are eighteen. Two years from now, we will reach twenty. Back when I was ten years old, twenty struck me as an advanced age. Before long, you will have turned into a respectable, middle-aged married woman, whereas I will be pleasant, elderly single Aunt Nell, arriving to stay with you during holidays. You will always reserve a spot for me, won’t you, Izzy dear? Naturally, not the guest room—unmarried women cannot aim for guest rooms, and I will be just as ’umble as Uriah Heep, perfectly happy with a small nook above the porch or adjacent to the parlor.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0017 }

“Nell, the things you say are so silly,” Isolde said with a laugh. “Your future husband will be a magnificent, attractive, and wealthy man—and every guest bedroom in Brierley won't come close to being grand enough for your stay—and you will look down on everyone you used to know as a girl.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0018 }

“It would be a shame; my nose is rather pretty, but I am afraid that upturning it would ruin its appearance,” Nell remarked while tapping the well-formed feature. “My attractive traits are not numerous enough for me to ruin the ones I possess; therefore, I guarantee I will not snub you, Isolde, even were I to wed the King of the Cannibal Islands.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0019 }

Giggling once more, the young women parted ways, as Isolde went back toward Pear Hill and Nell headed on foot to the Post Office. A letter was waiting for her at that location, and as Hugh Carrow caught up with her upon the bridge spanning the Lake of Glassy Waters, she beamed, animated by its contents.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0020 }

“Honora Hollis will be attending Wexcombe as well,” she cried out. “Is that not wonderful? I held out hope she might, though she doubted her father’s permission. He gave it, nonethless, and we shall room as companions. With a friend such as Honora beside me, I sense the strength to confront a marshaled host—or every Wexcombe professor arrayed in a single formidable line.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0021 }

“I believe Portmaris will suit us,” Hugh remarked. “People say it’s a pleasant old town, complete with the most splendid natural park anywhere. The landscape there is supposed to be grand, from what I’ve been told.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0022 }

“I wonder if it will be—can be—any more beautiful than this,” whispered Nell, gazing about herself with the affectionate, spellbound eyes belonging to people for whom “home” will forever remain the most gorgeous place on earth, regardless of how much lovelier the territories under foreign stars might be.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0023 }

The pair rested against the bridge over the ancient pond, fully absorbing the evening's magical atmosphere, right in the place where Nell had pulled herself out of her submerging Dory when Elaine drifted down toward Camelot. Although the western sky remained colored by the exquisite, purplish tint of sundown, the moon was climbing, causing the water to resemble a massive, silver fantasy beneath its illumination. Memories cast a delicate and delightful trance upon the two youths.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0024 }

“You are exceptionally silent, Nell,” Hugh remarked finally.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0025 }

“I feel terrified of speaking or making a move because I dread that this entire magnificent beauty might disappear like silence being shattered,” whispered Nell.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0026 }

Hugh abruptly placed his hand upon the delicate white hand that rested on the bridge's rail. The dark depth of his hazel eyes intensified, and his lips, which retained a boyish quality, parted to express the dream and hope stirring in his soul. Nell, however, pulled her hand back instantly and swung around. For her, the twilight's enchanting mood had vanished.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0027 }

“I must go home,” she cried out, pretending to be quite unconcerned. “Thirza’s head was aching this afternoon, and I feel certain the twins are up to some terrible trouble now. Truly, I ought not to have been absent for such a length of time.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0028 }

She talked without stopping or making much sense all the way to Grey Shutters lane, leaving poor Hugh with scarcely any opportunity to speak. Nell experienced a sense of relief once they said goodbye. Ever since that brief instant of understanding in the garden at Echo Cottage, a novel and hidden self-awareness had taken root in her heart concerning Hugh. An unfamiliar element had broken into their former, flawless, school-day companionship—an element that endangered its harmony.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0029 }

“I have never been pleased to witness Hugh’s departure until now,” she pondered, feeling partly resentful and partly sorrowful, while making her way up the lane by herself. “Should he persist in this foolishness, our connection will be ruined. It must not be ruined—I refuse to allow it. Oh, why are boys incapable of simply being reasonable!”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0030 }

Nell felt a troubled suspicion that it was hardly “sensible” for her to continue sensing the warm squeeze of Hugh’s hand on hers, just as clearly as when his had stayed there for that brief instant; and even less sensible that this feeling was not at all disagreeable—completely unlike the one that had accompanied a comparable gesture from Wilfred Mott, while she sat through a dance with him during a Pale Sands gathering three evenings earlier. Nell shuddered at the unpleasant memory. However, every issue regarding smitten suitors disappeared from her thoughts as she walked into the unpretentious, matter-of-fact setting of the Grey Shutters kitchen, where an eight-year-old boy wept bitterly upon the couch.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0031 }

“What is wrong, Robin?” inquired Nell, picking him up in her arms. “Where are Thirza and Lucy?”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0032 }

“Thirza is getting Lucy ready for bed,” weeping Robin said, “and my tears are because Lucy tumbled down the exterior cellar stairs, topsy-turvy, and stripped all the skin from her nose, and—”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0033 }

“Oh, well, refrain from weeping over it, dear. Naturally, she has your sympathy, yet your tears will not assist her in any way. By tomorrow, she will have recovered. Weeping is never of use to anybody, Robin-boy, and—”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0034 }

“It’s not because Lucy tumbled into the cellar that I’m weeping,” Robin stated, abruptly halting Nell’s well-intentioned sermon with growing resentment. “I’m weeping because I wasn’t present to witness her tumble. It appears to me that I’m constantly passing up one piece of enjoyment or another.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0035 }

“Oh, Robin!” Nell suppressed a wicked burst of laughter. “Do you think it is fun when poor little Lucy falls down the stairs and hurts herself?”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0036 }

“She didn’t get hurt very badly,” Robin said, in a defiant tone. “Naturally, I would have felt genuinely sorry if she had died, Nell. However, killing a Farrow isn't that simple. I suppose they resemble the Blewetts. Last Wednesday, Herb Scobie tumbled from the hayloft, going straight down the turnip chute into the box stall, which contained an awfully wild and ill-tempered horse, landing right beneath its hooves. Yet he managed to emerge alive, having broken merely three bones. Mrs. Sowerby claims that certain people cannot be killed even with a meat-axe. Nell, will Mrs. Sowerby be coming here tomorrow?”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0037 }

“Indeed, Robin, and my wish is that you will constantly treat her with great kindness and goodness.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0038 }

“I shall be good and nice. Nell, will she ever put me to bed at night, though?”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0039 }

“Maybe. For what reason?”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0040 }

“Because,” Robin stated with great conviction, “in the event that she does, I am not going to recite my prayers in her presence the way I recite them in yours, Nell.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0041 }

“Why not?”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0042 }

“Since I believe it would not be proper to pray in front of people we don’t know, Nell. While Lucy is free to recite hers to Mrs. Sowerby if she wishes, I refuse to do so. I intend to delay until she has departed before saying mine. Don’t you think that will be fine, Nell?”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0043 }

“Indeed, provided you are certain you will remember to speak those words, Robin-boy.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0044 }

“Oh, you can be sure I won't forget. Praying seems like a lot of fun to me. However, doing it by myself will not be quite as enjoyable as doing it with you. Nell, I wish you were staying here. Why you desire to depart and abandon us is beyond me.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0045 }

“It is not that I truly desire to do so, Robin, yet I perceive it as my duty to depart.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0046 }

“You do not have to go if you do not desire to. You are an adult. Nell, once I reach adulthood, I intend not to perform even a solitary task that I dislike.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0047 }

“You will discover throughout your entire life, Robin, that you are performing actions you would rather avoid.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0048 }

“I won’t,” Robin stated firmly. “Catch me! Right now I must perform tasks I dislike because you and Thirza will send me to bed otherwise. However, once I am an adult you will lack that power, and no one will exist to forbid me from doing things. What a great time I will have! Tell me, Nell, Milty Gammon claims his mother says you are attending college to find out if you can land a husband. Is that true, Nell? I wish to know.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0049 }

Nell felt a flash of anger for a moment. She then chuckled, recollecting that she could not be hurt by the unrefined coarseness of Mrs. Gammon’s mind and words.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0050 }

“No, Robin, I am not,” I replied, “as I intend to study, grow, and gain knowledge regarding numerous subjects.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0051 }

“Which items?”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0052 }

“‘Footwear and vessels and sealing wax, plus cabbages and monarchs,’”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0053 }

Nell was quoted.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0054 }

“How would you proceed, though, if you actually wished to capture a person? I desire to learn,” Robin continued stubbornly, as the topic clearly held a particular intrigue for him.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0055 }

“It would be best for you to inquire of Mrs. Gammon,” Nell remarked without thinking. “She probably understands the procedure better than me, in my opinion.”
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0056 }

“The next time she comes into my view, I shall,” Robin uttered with seriousness.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0057 }

“Robin! If you do!” yelled Nell, coming to understand her error.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0058 }

“However, I was simply following your instructions,” objected a hurt Robin.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0059 }

“You ought to go to sleep now,” declared Nell, as a means of escaping the difficulty.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0060 }

Following Robin's departure for bed, Nell strolled down to Victoria Island and remained seated by herself, enclosed in a delicate, moonlit dusk, as the surrounding water chuckled through a combined harmony of wind and brook. That brook had perpetually held a special place in Nell's heart. Over its shimmering current, she had fashioned numerous dreams throughout bygone times. She banished thoughts of enamored young men, the biting remarks from spiteful neighbors, and every dilemma belonging to her youthful life. Within her mind, she navigated across legendary oceans that lap against the remote, radiant coasts of “faery lands forlorn,” where forgotten Atlantis and Elysium rest, guided by the evening star toward the land of Heart’s Desire. Furthermore, she possessed greater wealth within those visions than in tangible life; because visible elements perish, whereas invisible elements endure forever.
{: #nw-v03-c01-p0061 }
